title: Open AI Glossary
status: Six working definitions; all repository proposals remain uncertified
introduction: A shared reference for research and engineering: compare meanings, inspect their boundaries, and follow the evidence.
Read in the order Workflow, Harness, Model, LLM, Agent, Schema. The sequence is a reading path, not a claim that all six form a single subtype hierarchy.
External evidence and repository certification are separate. Each working definition remains a proposal until a documented repository consensus decision is recorded.
source_policy: Research applicable formal institutional definitions first, then peer-reviewed papers, then industry standards, first-party documentation, preprints and academic materials, and finally Repository internal proposals.
Verify the original text, edition, publication status and context. A corporate engineering blog belongs to tier 3. Hosting a paper at a university does not change its publication type.
Prefer relevance over an unrelated authority. Preserve attributed disagreements, record source gaps, and do not turn a single paper into a consensus statement.
Citations accompany definitions, boundaries and typed relations. An editorial inference is marked explicitly; a source citation identifies its basis, not an endorsement of our inference.
adoption_policy: Yellow means Repository · Proposed / not certified. Green means Repository · Certified by consensus and requires an explicit unanimous repository decision, date, accessible decision link and evidence record. A merge, publication or authoritative external source does not establish repository certification.
license: Original handbook prose: CC BY 4.0. Build scripts and site code: MIT. Third-party sources retain their own rights.

terms.title: Workflow

definition.text: An arrangement of activities and control rules for carrying out a process. Distinguish the process, its description, and the system that executes it.

scope.text: This entry uses Workflow broadly for research and engineering. WfMC places it in business-process automation; its narrower historical definition does not itself define every scientific or Python workflow.

statement.text: WfMC describes partial or complete business-process automation, with work or information passed between participants under procedural rules.
A process definition specifies activities and routing; an instance enacts that definition for a particular case. The paper evaluates static control-flow patterns.
Anthropic calls predefined code paths coordinating LLMs and tools workflows, and contrasts them with model-directed agents. This is an architectural convention within LLM applications.

includes.text: Editorial example: a deterministic Python load → validate → transform → save pipeline has activities, dependencies and a completion condition. An LLM is unnecessary for our broader working usage.
Editorial example: a fixed retrieve → summarize → verify LLM pipeline is a workflow even when individual model outputs vary. Fixed control flow does not imply deterministic outputs.

excludes.text: A scheduler or execution engine is an implementation that runs work, not the process description itself.
A list of unrelated functions with no stated dependencies or process purpose fails our operational test.

ambiguities.text: Workflow may name a process arrangement, a stored definition, or a run in casual usage. State which object is meant before comparing implementations.
Predefined paths are not a universal requirement: WfMC distinguishes production workflows from ad-hoc workflows whose procedural rules can change during execution.
The 2003 patterns cover static control flow, not all resource allocation, exceptions or transaction semantics. Do not treat their scope as a universal exclusion rule.

operational.text: Repository test: identify a purpose, activities, dependencies or transition rules, and a completion or termination condition. Label the artifact as description, execution instance or executor. These are editorial criteria, not a quoted standard.

adaptation.text: Use Workflow for an organized process with explicit coordination rules, independent of whether its tasks are manual, deterministic code or model calls. Keep the executor separate from the process it realizes.

relations.condition: An LLM workflow uses an LLM for one or more tasks; many workflows use no language model.
A designed workflow may delegate an activity to an agent; this is composition, not a claim that every workflow is agentic.

source_gaps: Institutional scope gap: the historical WfMC definition concerns business automation. The broader Python example and our minimum operational test are explicit Repository proposals.
Retrieval limitation: indexed original excerpts verified the WfMC cover, glossary version and relevant definitions; direct retrieval of the two WfMC PDFs failed.

paragraphs.text: Sequence, dependencies, branches and loops describe the process. Validation and retry can also be workflow steps; a harness may enforce shared execution policies around them. This overlap does not make Harness a Workflow subtype. See the paired comparison in Harness for the schema-extraction example.

revisions.text: Researched and rewritten with attributed definitions, typed relations and an unratified Repository proposal.
Add the cited flow/governance comparison, overlap boundaries and illustrative experiment; Repository meaning remains proposed.
Scope the working definition and certification labels to this repository under Open AI Glossary. Citations and proposed status remain unchanged.

terms.title: Harness
terms.full_name: The execution layer around a model

definition.text: In agentic AI, a harness is software around a model that connects it to context and tools and controls execution. Sources differ on whether this means the control loop or the wider non-model runtime.

scope.text: Focus here is an agent runtime harness. An evaluation harness instead runs tasks and measures results; a framework or SDK supplies construction abstractions and may include a runtime. Shared naming does not make these identical objects.

statement.text: ASD uses harness for the non-LLM components of an agentic system, including connections to tools, data, memory and planning workflows, privileges and the control loop.

SWE-agent supplies a task-oriented interface for a language-model agent to navigate repositories, edit files and execute tests. This informs the runtime boundary; the paper is not treated as a general definition of Harness.
Anthropic separates session, harness and sandbox. Its harness drives the loop and routes model-requested tool calls; the sandbox executes them.
Macedo proposes an operational boundary against SDKs, frameworks, IDE plugins, evaluation scaffolds and orchestrators. This is one author’s definition proposal.

includes.text: Repository example: a running loop that assembles context, dispatches tools, records outcomes and applies stop or permission rules qualifies under our working definition.
A harness can realize fixed workflows as well as dynamic agent loops. Describe its actual control responsibilities rather than inferring them from a product name.

excludes.text: Model weights alone do not supply the surrounding runtime.
An SDK import or workflow diagram alone does not demonstrate a running harness. An evaluation runner is labeled evaluation harness unless it also has the claimed agent-runtime responsibilities.

ambiguities.text: ASD’s broad organizational boundary and Anthropic’s separated runtime components answer different questions. Neither establishes that a harness is a kind of process.
A runtime may be delivered inside an SDK or framework; packaging and execution responsibility are separate axes.

operational.text: Repository test: locate the running component responsible for model invocation, context/tool mediation, execution feedback and termination or privilege policy. State where session storage and tool execution live. If the software only constructs that component, label it a framework or SDK.

adaptation.text: Use agent harness for the model-surrounding execution layer that mediates context, tools, feedback and execution policy. For the proposed experiment, Workflow emphasizes flow and dependencies; Harness emphasizes controls and boundaries. Specify the policies and guarantees actually implemented.

relations.condition: A harness realizes or coordinates workflows; runtime-to-process is not strict subtype nesting.
When it supplies the running loop, tools and execution policy for an agent.
In an LLM-based agent runtime; evaluation harnesses and other harness usages have different scopes.

source_gaps: Peer-reviewed definition gap: this review did not establish a directly applicable peer-reviewed consensus definition of agent harness. The conceptual paper is a June 2026 preprint, not promoted to tier 2.

The NIST testing description establishes an additional, non-LLM usage; it does not supply a universal Harness definition. The flow/governance table and experimental example are editorial synthesis and an unratified internal proposal. The OpenAI reproducibility recipe is explicitly archived.

paragraphs.text: Workflow describes how work proceeds; Harness describes how execution is governed. This is an editorial distinction between responsibilities, not an official two-term taxonomy. A workflow can run within a harness, and one harness can realize several workflows.

The unqualified word harness is not exclusive to language models: NIST describes a healthcare test harness that executes and orchestrates testing services. Keep that usage separate from ASD's specifically agentic-AI scope.

left.text: What activities run, with which dependencies and control flow?

right.text: Which interfaces, permissions, execution policies and checks govern those activities?

left.text: No. Steps can involve people, deterministic code, LLM calls or agents.

right.text: No for the broader term. An agentic AI harness surrounds an LLM/agent; NIST's testing usage has another scope.

left.text: Sequence, branching, concurrency and iteration describe the process; a workflow need not be a simple linear chain.

right.text: May implement a loop or realize workflows; governance does not prescribe one universal step order.

left.text: Validation and retry branches may be steps in the process.

right.text: May enforce validation and retry budgets across calls, hold state and record failures. Exact capabilities must be specified.

left.text: Missing dependencies, unsuitable branches or an incorrect task decomposition.

right.text: Excessive permissions, unbounded execution, lost state or inadequate failure records.

paragraphs.text: For a paper and dataset, a proposed workflow is candidate discovery -> evidence retrieval -> attribute extraction -> deterministic schema assembly -> validation. Model calls and code can occupy different stages; this describes the task logic.

The proposed harness fixes the input snapshot and adapters, checks outputs against the declared JSON Schema dialect, and tracks field-to-evidence support separately. A structurally valid JSON object does not by itself prove that a field exists in the source or that an inferred attribute is true.

Example policies include a three-attempt limit, explicit token/time budgets, checkpointing, timeout and truncation handling, and recording model/configuration versions, prompts, outputs and failure reasons. Allow unknown only where the output contract permits it. These are proposed experiment controls, not mandatory properties of every harness.

For this experiment, an orchestrator schedules model/replicate/device assignments and task dependencies; the harness supplies the configured runtime and controls. They can overlap: NIST's test harness itself includes orchestration. This is a responsibility split, not three mutually exclusive software boxes.

The same extract -> validate -> retry code can play both roles. Describing its branch and loop structure is a workflow view; enforcing a shared attempt budget, validation contract and failure record is a harness view. The distinction follows responsibility, not Python syntax.

The harness metaphor suggests bounded, observable and recoverable execution. It does not establish that the model becomes deterministic or always correct, or that every harness actually enforces its advertised policies. An implementation must test those policies and state the limits of its guarantees.

Recording inputs, configuration, model versions and seeds supports an auditable experiment setup. It is not a universal promise of identical outputs: OpenAI's archived 2023 example explicitly allows differing responses even when seed, request parameters and system fingerprint match. That provider-specific example is not current API guidance for every model.

terms.title: Model

definition.text: Model has several scopes: a representation of a subject; an executable representation; or, in AI, the inference component transforming inputs into outputs. State the scope before using the term.

scope.text: A model need not be learned. NASA’s modeling-and-simulation sense includes conceptual representations, while the AI terminology concerns an inference component within a system.

statement.text: NASA defines a model as a description or representation of a system, entity, phenomenon or process. It separately defines conceptual and computational models.

A computational model is a usable implementation of a conceptual model, including mathematical, numerical, logical or qualitative representations. Executability alone does not specify what is represented.
The EU-U.S. terminology identifies a model as a core AI-system component that infers outputs from inputs. This context is narrower than every possible software function.

includes.text: Editorial examples: a conceptual climate description and its numerical simulation fit representation-oriented usage; a trained classifier fits learned inference usage. These are distinct cases under a broad term.
An LLM is one specialized learned model, rather than a synonym for all models.

excludes.text: “Any input → output” is insufficient as a universal definition: it omits what the artifact represents and collapses ordinary utilities into model terminology. We retain it only as an internal proposal.
An application containing a model, orchestration and tools is a system; the model name should identify its inference component.

ambiguities.text: In learned-model usage, identify the fitted parameters and inference rule; in conceptual-model usage, identify the referent and assumptions. Do not silently require training for all models.
A fixed formula may be a model when it represents a stated phenomenon. Being deterministic neither establishes nor prevents that role.

operational.text: Repository test: record the intended sense, represented subject or inference task, assumptions, inputs and outputs if executable, and whether parameters were learned. For learned models, distinguish the checkpoint from deployment and orchestration.

adaptation.text: Default to a representation or inference component with an explicit subject or task. Use “learned model” when training matters. The broader “any input-to-output mapping” guide remains a pending alternative, not our universal definition.

source_gaps: Scope gap: NASA’s general representation terminology applies to modeling and simulation; it does not settle every AI use. The EU-U.S. AI meaning and the internal mapping proposal are shown separately.

revisions.text: Researched and rewritten with attributed definitions, typed relations and an unratified Repository proposal.
Scope the working definition and certification labels to this repository under Open AI Glossary. Citations and proposed status remain unchanged.

terms.title: LLM

definition.text: A large language model is a deep learning language model trained on very large textual datasets. It is a kind of Model; its complete application or agent runtime is a separate system.

scope.text: This page concerns learned language models, including text generation and representation uses. The word “large” needs a stated scale and comparison context.

statement.text: The second edition emphasizes deep learning and extremely large text datasets, and includes models that generate text or form representations useful for downstream tasks.

Brown and colleagues study an autoregressive model with 175 billion parameters alongside smaller models. Its training corpus mixes web sources, books and Wikipedia; that recipe is an example, not a definition.

includes.text: A trained text-generation checkpoint is a model artifact; adding retrieval, tools and execution control creates a larger application around it.
Representation-producing language models are within the cited institutional usage; generation is not its only permitted behavior.

excludes.text: A corpus alone is training material, not a trained model. A tool-connected assistant is not identical to the language model inside it.
No universal parameter cutoff is established by the sources used here. Report parameters, training tokens and the relevant comparison rather than inventing a threshold.

ambiguities.text: The institutional definition foregrounds textual training. For a multimodal product, specify its language-model component and additional modalities instead of assuming the same definition covers the whole system.
Training a model and conditioning an inference call are different operations: the GPT-3 few-shot experiments add examples in context without gradient updates.

operational.text: Repository test: identify the learned model artifact, language task and objective, available training-material evidence, and reported scale. Record unknown proprietary details as unknown. Separately identify any tokenizer, serving system, tools and controller.

adaptation.text: Use LLM for a learned language-model component at a documented large scale. Avoid reducing the term to corpus size alone or using it as the name for a tool-using system. No minimum parameter count is ratified by the repository.

relations.condition: Within learned AI-model usage: an LLM is a specialized language model, hence a Model.

source_gaps: Scale gap: the institutional definition supplies qualitative scale, not a universal threshold; a concrete GPT-3 size cannot settle the category for all architectures.

revisions.text: Researched and rewritten with attributed definitions, typed relations and an unratified Repository proposal.
Scope the working definition and certification labels to this repository under Open AI Glossary. Citations and proposed status remain unchanged.

terms.title: Agent

definition.text: In general computing, an agent is a situated system with some control over its actions, responsiveness to its environment and goal-directed behavior. LLM-based agents are one implementation, not the whole category.

scope.text: Begin with general software or hardware agency. For LLM engineering, explicitly identify the model, action interface and feedback loop; access to a tool alone does not settle agency.

statement.text: Wooldridge and Jennings characterize a weak notion through autonomy, social ability, reactivity and pro-activeness. This influential characterization is attributed, not presented as the only universal test.
The NCCoE concept paper describes autonomous decisions and actions under limited human supervision toward goals. It is a draft project-scoping document, not a final general-agent standard.
Anthropic distinguishes predefined workflows from agents whose LLM dynamically directs the process and tool use. Its usage is narrower than general agent theory.

includes.text: Editorial example: a goal-directed robot controller can be an agent without an LLM. A software agent can act through commands in a virtual environment.
Bounded autonomy can coexist with approval gates. Record which decisions the system controls and which require a person.

excludes.text: A bare text-completion call does not, by itself, show goal-directed interaction with an environment under our test.
A fixed tool pipeline is not automatically an agent in the dynamic-control engineering sense, even if it contains an LLM and an API.

ambiguities.text: Planning, long-term memory and self-learning are not universal prerequisites in our working definition. Capability claims should be tested separately from the name Agent.

We retain autonomy, goal direction, environment feedback and action as Repository criteria. Social ability is explicit in the classical weak notion, but is not a mandatory gate in our narrower operational proposal.

operational.text: Repository test: identify a goal, observations, an action interface, the decisions controlled by the system, and how outcomes affect later actions. For an LLM-based agent, trace a model-selected action, its execution and returned feedback. State stopping and approval conditions.

adaptation.text: Use Agent for a system with bounded autonomy, a goal, environment feedback and an ability to act. Use LLM-based agent when an LLM participates in selecting actions. The agent uses a model; it is not classified as an LLM subtype.

relations.condition: For LLM-based agents only; general agents need not use a language model.
When a computational model supplies inference or action selection; this is a component relation.

source_gaps: Institutional definition gap: the NIST material checked is a draft identity/authorization concept paper. No final, general-agent institutional definition was established in this review; the classical peer-reviewed account remains central.

paragraphs.text: An LLM-based agent places a language model within an action-and-observation system. ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions that obtain external information, allowing later reasoning to respond to outcomes. It is one architecture, not a requirement that every agent expose a chain of thought.
Distinguish choosing an action, granting permission and executing it. A model’s proposed tool call does not itself execute a tool; the surrounding runtime provides that capability.

revisions.text: Researched and rewritten with attributed definitions, typed relations and an unratified Repository proposal.
Scope the working definition and certification labels to this repository under Open AI Glossary. Citations and proposed status remain unchanged.

terms.title: Schema

definition.text: A schema describes how data is organized and what its fields mean, with structural or value constraints where specified. State the data model and dialect: the exact obligations depend on the schema language.

scope.text: Here, schema means a data-description artifact used for interpretation or validation. Psychological schemata and prediction models are outside this entry.

definition_views.label: Institutional terminology
definition_views.context: CNSSI 4009-2022, reproduced by NIST CSRC; information-security context

statement.text: CNSSI describes an object through its organization, field syntax, meanings and associated metadata. This is broader than a list of column names.
XSD separates abstract schema components from their XML schema documents; a validator applies a conforming schema to an XML instance.
JSON Schema describes an instance using an object or boolean schema. Assertions constrain instances; annotations supply information for applications.

definition_views.label: Data-derived summary
definition_views.context: Goldman and Widom, VLDB 1997; semistructured databases

statement.text: DataGuides provide structural summaries generated from a database, serving as dynamic schemas for browsing and querying. Their scope is observed structure in that database.

includes.text: Named fields, types, permitted structure and explicit constraints; meanings or metadata may also be documented. A schema need not specify every aspect of domain interpretation.

excludes.text: A particular record is a data instance, not the rules applied to it. For example, {"temperature": 23.5} supplies a value; a schema separately describes the property and its constraints.
A validator is software that applies a schema. The schema itself is neither that execution nor an entire workflow.

ambiguities.text: Schema may mean declared requirements or a summary inferred from existing data. A DataGuide follows the database; a declared contract can reject data that fails its requirements. Label which direction is intended.
The schema/instance distinction is a role distinction: a JSON schema is itself an instance when checked against a meta-schema. JSON syntax alone does not identify that role.

operational.text: Identify the described population, schema version/dialect, fields and constraints; distinguish declared rules from observed patterns and unknowns. Show how an example instance is interpreted or checked without treating that example as evidence for every possible record.

adaptation.text: Proposed Repository meaning: an explicit, versioned description of data structure, field meanings and stated constraints. Record whether it is declared, recovered from a specification, or inferred from observed data, together with evidence and unresolved coverage.

relations.condition: Supports a workflow at data-interpretation or validation boundaries; it supplies a description or contract, not the executing control flow. This is a supporting-artifact relation, not a subtype.

paragraphs.text: Schema extraction is the process; a recovered or inferred schema is its output. DataGuides illustrate inference from instances. Recovering an explicitly declared schema is a different evidence task from generalizing observed records.

For Repository work, retain source-to-field evidence and label observed, declared and inferred constraints. An absent field in a sample does not by itself establish that the field is forbidden; a structural summary alone does not prove complete intended semantics.

source_gaps: The applicable institutional definition was verified through the NIST reproduction; the linked original CNSSI document was not retrievable in this review.

The peer-reviewed DataGuides example supports one semistructured-data approach. This review does not establish a universal definition of schema extraction across paper, database and metadata workflows.

revisions.text: Initial cited Schema entry; separates data instances, validation and extraction. Repository meaning is an unratified editorial proposal.
Scope the working definition and certification labels to this repository under Open AI Glossary. Citations and proposed status remain unchanged.

sections.title: Workflow and Harness
paragraphs: Initial proposal: Workflow is a general arrangement of work; deterministic Python code as well as LLM-based work can participate in a workflow.

Initial proposal: a harness is a workflow designed for an LLM or agent. Editorial revision for discussion: distinguish the execution layer from the process it supports. This edition uses supports/orchestrates rather than declaring a Harness is-a Workflow relationship.

sections.title: Model and LLM
paragraphs: Initial proposal: any input-to-output mapping may be called a model. This remains an intentionally broad, unratified interpretation, not a universal external definition.

Working revision: specify whether model means a representation, an executable representation, or a learned inference component. An LLM is a learned language model; its training, scale and scope should be described rather than reduced to an arbitrary parameter threshold.

sections.title: Agent
paragraphs: Initial proposal: an agent builds on an LLM and external tools, with its distinguishing attributes still to be decided.

Working revision: reserve the general term for systems with bounded autonomy, goal-directed behavior, environmental feedback and an ability to act. Describe an LLM-based agent as one particular implementation using an LLM. Planning, persistent memory and self-learning are optional capabilities, not automatic universal requirements.

sections.title: Editorial and adoption policy
paragraphs: Check external evidence in the fixed order: applicable institutional definitions, peer-reviewed papers, industry standards or first-party documents or preprints or academic materials, then internal proposals. Preserve uncertainty and differing scopes.

Use cited statements, typed relations and a quiet reading layout. Strict nesting is reserved for supported is-a relations. All proposals in this guide are unratified; only a documented consensus decision may authorize green adoption tags.

sections.title: Schema: an unratified editorial extension
paragraphs: Proposed extension: use schema for an explicit, versioned description of data structure, field meanings and stated constraints. Keep the data instance, the description and the validator separate; the same document can occupy different roles under a meta-schema.

Schema extraction is a process that recovers declarations or infers a description from evidence. Record the input population, source-to-field evidence, dialect/version, observed versus declared or inferred constraints, and unresolved coverage. A sample is not proof of every permitted record or intended semantic rule.

sections.title: Workflow and Harness: flow and governance proposal
paragraphs: Proposed distinction: Workflow describes how work proceeds, including sequence, dependencies, branches and loops. Harness describes how execution is governed through interfaces, policies, validation, state, recovery and observability. These are overlapping responsibilities, not mutually exclusive categories or a universal subtype taxonomy.

Illustrative schema-extraction workflow: candidate discovery, evidence retrieval, attribute extraction, deterministic schema assembly and validation. This is a proposed teaching example, not a report of an implemented or evaluated Repository system.

Proposed experimental harness policies: standardize input snapshots and model adapters, bound attempts and resource consumption, permit an explicit unknown value only where the declared schema allows it, distinguish evidence support from structural validation, checkpoint progress and record inputs, model/configuration versions, prompts, outputs and failure reasons.

For this example, orchestration assigns models, replicates, devices and dependencies. An experimental harness supplies the configured execution and recording environment. These roles may live in the same implementation. Recording experimental conditions helps audit and repeat a setup; it does not establish that every output will be identical or correct.
